newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan body asks court to declare realtor bankrupt.
newsitem.headline: Japan body asks court to declare realtor bankrupt.

text.p: The Housing Loan Administration Corp (HLAC), a body set up to collect problem loans run up by Japan's failed "jusen" mortgage firms, said on Tuesday it had asked an Osaka court to declare realtor Sueno Kosan bankrupt.
Sueno Kosan is a major borrower from the mortgage firms. The loan collection body announced the move in a statement.
Kohei Nakabo, president of the corporation, told reporters recently that the HLAC was considering taking such action.
Japanese media also reported recently that the corporation was considering such a move because of alleged attempts to transfer Sueno Kosan assets to affiliates.
In September, Sueno Kosan chief Kenichi Sueno pleaded guilty in the Osaka District Court to charges that he and some aides hid assets to prevent them being seized by creditors.
Japanese media have said that estimated total liabilities at the Osaka-based firm were around 560 billion yen on a parent company basis and 670 billion yen on a group basis.

Sueno Kosan is not a listed company. If it is declared bankrupt, it would be one of the biggest Japanese insolvencies on record, financial industry sources said. They said that if the firm goes under, creditor non-bank financial institutions could face difficulties.

The Sueno group was the second-largest borrower from the mortgage firms. Media reports have said it borrowed 236.7 billion yen from five of the seven jusen and about 300 billion yen from 10 other financial institutions.

This would be the first time for the loan-collecting body to seek the bankruptcy of a major borrower of the seven failed housing loan firms since the government adopted a controversial scheme to wind up the jusen companies.
The firms collapsed under the weight of property loans made during the "bubble" era lending boom of the 1980s.

Noboru Matsuda, governor of the Deposit Insurance Corp of Japan (DIC), which supervises the loan-collecting body, said in a statement that the DIC has no intention of seeking the bankrupcy of every borrower of the jusen firms.
But he said such action would be inevitable for some "malignant" borrowers like Sueno, which he accused of repeatedly attempting to hide assets.
Matsuda said that the DIC hopes that speedy and appropriate legal procedures will be taken in the Sueno case.
Sueno Kosan officials were not immediately available for comment.
